newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: FOCUS-Malaysia sets rules to force finance firms growth.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Malaysia sets rules to force finance firms growth.

text.p: Malaysia's central bank on Monday announced new requirements for finance companies that will force them to grow through raising capital or mergers.

Bank Negara Malaysia announced that finance companies must raise their shareholders' funds to at least 350 million ringgit ($139 million) by January 1, 1998 to remain eligible for trading in the interbank money market.
The requirement would be further increased to 600 million ringgit by January 1, 1999, Bank Negara Governor Ahmad Mohd Don said.
"In general, size has become an increasingly important factor to gain competitiveness," the governor said.
He had earlier spoken on the subject at the Forex Association of Malaysia's annual dinner on Saturday, but his speech was not released to the media until Monday.
"Among the interbank money market players, I note that a number of institutions are still under-capitalised. I would urge these institutions to build up their size and capacity," he said.
The central bank has a policy of encouraging the creation of large banking firms.
Ahmad said the increase in the capital requirement for finance companies would enable them to attain Tier-I status under Malaysia's two-tier system for banking institutions.
Tier-I banks, merchant banks and finance companies are allowed to operate in a more liberal regulatory environment.

Apart from capital, Tier-I institutions also have to meet stringent requirements under the CAMEL rating framework, which evaluates a firm's capital adequacy, asset quality, management efficiency, earning performance and liquidity position.

Among the 40 prominent finance companies, only three have so far achieved Tier-I status, according to the Association of Finance Companies of Malaysia. They are Hong Leong Finance Bhd, Mayban Finance Bhd and Public Finance Bhd.
"Not having access to the interbank market will be a big blow to small finance companies," said the head of money dealing at a large finance company.
"(The) interbank market is a source of relatively cheap funds. More importantly, funds are always available," he said.
Money market dealers said this meant that smaller finance companies will have to depend exclusively on their deposits to meet lending and other requirements.
Bankers said while Bank Negara's urgings have triggered mergers and capital raising exercises among banks, finance companies have been slow to follow.

This year, after taking over United Malayan Banking Corp Bhd (UMBC), now renamed Sime Bank, Malaysian conglomerate Sime Darby, announced plans recently to acquire a majority stake in Oriental Bank Bhd.
Also, stockbroker Rashid Hussain Bhd announced a deal to acquire Kwong Yik Bank and merge it with its associate DCB Holdings Bhd's banking unit to create the third largest bank in the country.

Bank of Commerce, part of Commerce Asset Holdings Bhd said early this month it was in the market to raise 1.2 billion ringgit, a move that has fueled speculation about a possible merger with another bank.
To achieve Tier-I status, banks should have minimum shareholders' funds of 500 million ringgit, which should be increased to one billion by the year 2000.
-- Kuala Lumpur newsroom (603-230 8911)
($1=2.52 ringgit)
